regions.name: Prefrontal Cortex (PFC)
regions.summary: The brain’s command center for sustaining attention, inhibiting distractions, and regulating behavior and emotions. In ADHD it is often underactive or inefficiently connected, and it needs optimal levels of dopamine and norepinephrine to work properly.

groups.name: Cognitive / Executive Functions
groups.explanation: Often underactive or inefficiently connected in ADHD; relies on optimal dopamine and norepinephrine levels. Disruption leads to distractibility, forgetfulness, impulsivity, and poor planning.
groups.adhd: Disruption here produces the classic ADHD profile: distractibility, forgetfulness, impulsivity, and poor planning.

groups.name: Emotional / Social Functions
groups.explanation: The PFC’s role in emotional regulation is critical; when impaired in ADHD, it contributes to emotional dysregulation and impulsivity often seen alongside core symptoms.
groups.adhd: Impairment fuels emotional dysregulation, hot-headed impulsivity, and trouble with social judgment and delayed gratification.

groups.name: Motor Functions
groups.explanation: The PFC contributes to the planning phase of movement, working in concert with motor cortices and subcortical structures.
groups.adhd: Weak movement planning adds to clumsiness and poorly sequenced actions, compounding restless, hyperactive behavior.

groups.name: Integrative / Language Functions
groups.explanation: The PFC acts as a hub, coordinating inputs from multiple brain areas to support complex cognition and behavior.
groups.adhd: A noisy hub fails to integrate instructions and context — verbal directions get lost and multi-step tasks fall apart.

functions.title: Regulating aggression and socially inappropriate behavior
Motor planning and control of voluntary movement
Integrating information from other brain regions

regions.name: Striatum (Basal Ganglia)
regions.summary: Part of the frontostriatal network linking the PFC to deeper structures. It selects and executes appropriate actions while suppressing inappropriate ones, and lays down habits through reward-modulated learning. Structural and functional differences — particularly in the caudate nucleus — are consistently found in ADHD.

groups.name: Action Selection and Inhibition
groups.explanation: Part of the frontostriatal network; structural and functional differences (especially in the caudate nucleus) contribute to problems with inhibition in ADHD.
groups.adhd: A weakened brake lets inappropriate actions slip through as hyperactivity, restlessness, and impulsivity.

groups.name: Learning and Memory
groups.explanation: The striatum generates patterns for movement and cognitive processes, learning and laying down memories important for guiding actions. Repeated firing leads to habit development, modulated by reward-related dopamine signals.
groups.adhd: Altered reward-dopamine modulation skews habits toward immediately rewarding behavior and makes steady routines harder to establish.

groups.name: Cognitive Functions
groups.explanation: The basal ganglia participate in circuits involving cortex and thalamus that support motor control, reward processing, and procedural learning.
groups.adhd: Disrupted cortex–basal-ganglia–thalamus loops degrade working memory and set-shifting, so switching approach mid-task is difficult.

functions.title: Building higher-order representations of sequential actions

regions.name: Cerebellum
regions.summary: Beyond its classic role in motor coordination, it contributes to attention, executive function, and cognitive and emotional processes via connections with the cerebrum. Many people with ADHD show differences in cerebellar volume and connectivity — and motor coordination difficulties are common.

groups.name: Motor Control and Coordination
groups.explanation: The cerebellum constantly compares intended movement with actual movement and makes appropriate adjustments. It coordinates motor acts so they happen in harmony, without shocks.
groups.adhd: Poor comparison of intended versus actual movement shows up as clumsiness, restlessness, and ill-timed actions.

groups.name: Motor Learning
groups.explanation: The cerebellum participates actively in learning processes of motor tasks and memory storage.
groups.adhd: Slower motor learning keeps everyday actions effortful — skills and routines take longer to become automatic.

groups.name: Non-Motor (Cognitive / Emotional) Functions
groups.explanation: The neocerebellum is linked to non-sensorimotor functions including perceptual, cognitive, and emotional processes. Its role in nonmotor cognitive and affective functions is increasingly recognized.
groups.adhd: Disrupted cerebello-cerebral loops weaken attention, working memory, verbal fluency, and emotional processing — the cognitive side of ADHD.

functions.title: Planning coordinated, properly timed movement sequences
Comparing intended movement with actual movement and making adjustments
Executive tasks (random number generation, complex decision-making)

regions.name: Corpus Callosum
regions.summary: A thick band of white matter joining the two hemispheres. Research shows white-matter integrity differences in ADHD, which may slow the communication between regions that attention and motor regulation depend on.

groups.name: Interhemispheric Integration
groups.explanation: The corpus callosum is crucial for bilateral integration of sensory, motor, or higher cognitive functions. Research on split-brain patients demonstrated its role in interhemispheric transfer of visual information.
groups.adhd: Slower transfer between hemispheres makes attention less stable and coordination between brain systems less reliable.

groups.name: Functional Lateralization
groups.explanation: The corpus callosum can have both inhibitory and excitatory effects on the contralateral hemisphere. Its microstructure predicts interhemispheric inhibition function.
groups.adhd: Faulty interhemispheric inhibition lets the wrong hemisphere intrude — responses slip out poorly filtered.

groups.name: Metacontrol
groups.explanation: This phenomenon is linked to how different types of processing in the two hemispheres are combined to yield a single behavioral response.
groups.adhd: When the hemispheres cannot fuse their processing into one response, behavior turns inconsistent and poorly unified.

functions.title: Bilateral integration of sensory, motor, or higher cognitive functions
Combining different types of processing in the two hemispheres to yield a single behavioral response

regions.name: Limbic System (Amygdala and related structures)
regions.summary: Emotion, reward, memory, and survival circuitry — including the amygdala — shows altered connectivity in ADHD. This impairment in the affective network is linked to the emotional dysregulation, impulsivity, and conduct problems often seen alongside core symptoms.

groups.name: Emotion Processing
groups.explanation: The amygdala is an essential component of the circuitry underlying fear-related responses. It plays a key role in emotional behavior, linked to both fear responses and feelings of pleasure.
groups.adhd: An over-reactive amygdala tags ordinary setbacks with outsized emotional value — small frustrations feel like emergencies.

groups.name: Memory and Learning
groups.explanation: The amygdala is involved in forming and storing memories for emotive events. Long-term synaptic plasticity of inputs to the amygdala underlies acquisition of fear memory.
groups.adhd: Strongly encoded emotional memories mean fear and frustration condition quickly, fueling outsized reactions to reminders of past failures.

groups.name: Survival Behaviors
groups.explanation: The limbic system is implicated in higher integration of visceral, olfactory, and somatic information as well as homeostatic responses including fundamental survival behaviors.
groups.adhd: Survival circuitry running hot amplifies urgency and restlessness — everything feels pressing and nothing can wait.

groups.name: Social and Autonomic Functions
groups.explanation: Cells responding to complex aspects of social communications are found in the amygdala. The limbic system coordinates visceral reactions with emotion and motivation.
groups.adhd: Misread social signals plus amplified bodily arousal drive conflict, emotional outbursts, and trouble calming down.

functions.title: Assigning emotional significance or value to sensory information
Forming and storing memories for emotive events

networkNote.explanation: ADHD is a network disorder — symptoms arise from disrupted circuits connecting these regions, not from a single area failing.
